subject: chemistry_2
question_text: Give the hybridization of sulphur in the following: a) SO₂ b) SO₃ c) SF₄ d) SF₆

verification.note: The 1+1 mark split is a CLAIM, not the board's, until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it; the question itself is sourced, not invented. Source: "FAST TRACK IPE for Sr. Students", chemistry half, book pp.84-86, sub-box "VIA GROUP ELEMENTS" of printed chapter 7; this is VSAQ 3 of that sub-box, book p.85. Neither the two-book union check nor a board back-test was possible for Chemistry-II: the TSBIE Basic Learning Material on hand is physics-only and first-year, and no second-year chemistry paper is in the corpus. BOOK ERROR (label order): the question is printed a) SO₂ b) SO₃ c) SF₄ d) SF₆, but the printed answer is lettered "(a) SO₂ → Sp², (b) SF₄ → Sp³d, (c) SO₃ → Sp², (d) SF₆ → Sp³d²". The letters b and c are swapped against the question. The four hybridisation values themselves are correct; only the lettering is wrong. This card answers in the QUESTION's order. The book also prints the hybridisation with a capital S, "Sp²"; the accepted notation is lower case, sp². BOOK GAP: the printed answer gives no shapes, and does not say why sulphur can expand its octet while oxygen cannot. Both are written on this card. CROSS-BANK OVERLAP: Chemistry-I card ts_ipe_c1_cb_sf6_hybridisation is a 4-mark SAQ on SF₆ hybridisation with the orbital ladder and a diagram. This card is a different question in a different paper and stays at the 2-mark level, listing hybridisation and shape only. QUESTION WORDING: printed without a colon, "Give the hybridization of sulphur in the following a) SO₂ b) SO₃ c) SF₄ d) SF₆"; a colon was added here for readability. Nothing else in the wording was changed.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: SO₂ and SO₃
lines: a) SO₂ : sulphur is sp² hybridised.
Three sp² orbitals hold two bond pairs and
one lone pair, so the shape is angular.
b) SO₃ : sulphur is sp² hybridised.
Three sp² orbitals hold three bond pairs and
no lone pair, so the shape is trigonal
steps.why: The hybridisation is counted from the number of sigma bonds plus lone pairs on the central atom, never from the number of oxygen atoms. SO₂ has two sigma bonds and one lone pair, and SO₃ has three sigma bonds and no lone pair. Both come to three, so both are sp². The pi bonds are not counted.
common_mistakes: Counting the double bonds and writing sp³ for SO₃. Only sigma bonds and lone pairs are counted; the pi bond does not use a hybrid orbital.
Writing the same shape for both. Both are sp², but the lone pair in SO₂ makes it angular while SO₃ is trigonal planar.
steps.memory_tip: Count sigma bonds plus lone pairs. Three of them means sp², whether the molecule is SO₂ or SO₃.
steps.margin_note: The hybridisation label is the marked item. Shapes are supporting content and cost nothing to add.

steps.label: SF₄ and SF₆

lines.text: c) SF₄ : sp³d      d) SF₆ : sp³d²

lines: In SF₄ five sp³d orbitals are formed. Four
hold bond pairs and the fifth holds a lone
pair, so the shape is see-saw.
In SF₆ six sp³d² orbitals are formed and all
six hold bond pairs, so the shape is
Sulphur can do this because its third shell
has empty 3d orbitals. Oxygen has no d
orbitals in its second shell, so OF₄ and OF₆
steps.why: SF₄ has four sigma bonds and one lone pair, which is five, so one d orbital is used and the hybridisation is sp³d. SF₆ has six sigma bonds and no lone pair, so two d orbitals are used and it is sp³d². The last two lines are the exception that makes the group trend honest: sulphur, selenium and tellurium expand the octet, oxygen never does, because the second shell has no d orbitals at all.
common_mistakes: Writing sp³d for SF₆. Six positions need six hybrid orbitals, which is sp³d².
Forgetting the lone pair in SF₄ and calling it tetrahedral. Four bonds plus one lone pair is five positions, so it is see-saw inside a trigonal bipyramid.
Saying oxygen forms OF₆ by the same rule. Oxygen has no d orbitals in the second shell, so its covalency stops at two.
steps.memory_tip: SF₄ has four bonds plus one lone pair, so five, so sp³d. SF₆ has six bonds, so six, so sp³d².
steps.margin_note: Both labels together earn this mark. The oxygen line is not marked but is the sentence an examiner reads as understanding.

insider_note: Marks are given for the four labels, not for the explanation, so write all four first and then add the shapes. The label most often written wrong is SF₄, because students forget its lone pair.
